editorialPolicy: Public-domain original English verse. Excerpts are contiguous source lines; indentation and blank stanza lines are removed, but wording and punctuation follow the cited edition. Titles may use conventional work names instead of anthology headings.

treasury.title: The Golden Treasury, selected by Francis Turner Palgrave

browning.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese, 1906 Caradoc Press edition

byron-beauty.title: Representative Poetry Online, University of Toronto; Hebrew Melodies (1815), Works (1832–33)

poems.author: Lord Byron
poems.title: She Walks in Beauty
poems.text:
She walks in beauty, like the night
Of cloudless climes and starry skies;
And all that's best of dark and bright
Meet in her aspect and her eyes:
Thus mellow'd to that tender light
Which heaven to gaudy day denies.

poems.author: Christopher Marlowe
poems.title: The Passionate Shepherd to His Love
poems.text:
Come live with me and be my Love,
And we will all the pleasures prove
That hills and valleys, dale and field,
And all the craggy mountains yield.
poems.sourceHeading: THE PASSIONATE SHEPHERD TO HIS LOVE.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: It Was a Lover and His Lass
poems.text:
It was a lover and his lass
With a hey, and a ho, and a hey-nonino!
That o'er the green cornfield did pass,
In the spring time, the only pretty ring time,
When birds do sing hey ding a ding:
Sweet lovers love the Spring.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 97
poems.text:
How like a winter hath my absence been
From Thee, the pleasure of the fleeting year!
What freezings have I felt, what dark days seen,
What old December's bareness everywhere!

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 29
poems.text:
Yet in these thoughts my self almost despising,
Haply I think on Thee—and then my state,
Like to the lark at break of day arising
From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven's gate;
For thy sweet love remember'd, such wealth brings
That then I scorn to change my state with kings.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 109
poems.text:
For nothing this wide universe I call,
Save thou, my rose, in it thou art my all.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 104
poems.text:
To me, fair Friend, you never can be old,
For as you were when first your eye I eyed
Such seems your beauty still. Three winters cold
Have from the forests shook three summers' pride;
Three beauteous springs to yellow autumn turn'd,
In process of the seasons have I seen,
Three April perfumes in three hot Junes burn'd,
Since first I saw you fresh which yet are green.

poems.author: Henry Constable
poems.title: Diaphenia
poems.text:
Diaphenia like the daffadowndilly,
White as the sun, fair as the lily,
Heigh ho, how do I love thee!
I do love thee as my lambs
Are belovéd of their dams;
How blest were I if thou would'st prove me.

poems.author: Thomas Lodge
poems.title: Rosaline
poems.text:
Her eyes are sapphires set in snow,
Resembling heaven by every wink;
The Gods do fear whenas they glow,
And I do tremble when I think
Heigh ho, would she were mine!

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 18
poems.text:
Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date:

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 106
poems.text:
So all their praises are but prophecies
Of this our time, all, you prefiguring;
And for they look'd but with divining eyes,
They had not skill enough your worth to sing:
For we, which now behold these present days,
Have eyes to wonder, but lack tongues to praise.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 116
poems.text:
Let me not to the marriage of true minds
Admit impediments. Love is not love
Which alters when it alteration finds,
Or bends with the remover to remove:—
O no! it is an ever-fixéd mark
That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
It is the star to every wandering bark
Whose worth's unknown, although his height be taken.

poems.author: Philip Sidney
poems.title: My True Love Hath My Heart
poems.text:
My true love hath my heart, and I have his,
By just exchange one to the other given:
I hold his dear, and mine he cannot miss,
There never was a better bargain driven:
My true love hath my heart, and I have his.

poems.author: Joshua Sylvester
poems.title: Love’s Omnipresence
poems.text:
Were you the earth, dear Love, and I the skies,
My love should shine on you like to the sun,
And look upon you with ten thousand eyes
Till heaven wax'd blind, and till the world were done.
Whereso'er I am, below, or else above you,
Whereso'er you are, my heart shall truly love you.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: O Mistress Mine
poems.text:
O Mistress mine, where are you roaming?
O, stay and hear! your true-love's coming
That can sing both high and low;
Trip no further, pretty sweeting,
Journeys end in lovers' meeting—
Every wise man's son doth know.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 73
poems.text:
—This thou perceiv'st, which makes thy love more strong,
To love that well which thou must leave ere long.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 30
poems.text:
—But if the while I think on thee, dear friend,
All losses are restored, and sorrows end.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Take, O Take Those Lips Away
poems.text:
Take O take those lips away
That so sweetly were forsworn,
And those eyes, the break of day,
Lights that do mislead the morn:
But my kisses bring again,
Bring again—
Seals of love, but seal'd in vain,
Seal'd in vain!

poems.author: Edmund Waller
poems.title: Go, Lovely Rose!
poems.text:
Go, lovely Rose!
Tell her, that wastes her time and me,
That now she knows,
When I resemble her to thee,
How sweet and fair she seems to be.

poems.author: Ben Jonson
poems.title: To Celia
poems.text:
Drink to me only with thine eyes,
And I will pledge with mine;
Or leave a kiss but in the cup
And I'll not look for wine.
The thirst that from the soul doth rise
Doth ask a drink divine;
But might I of Jove's nectar sup,
I would not change for thine.

poems.author: Robert Herrick
poems.title: Upon Julia’s Clothes
poems.text:
Whenas in silks my Julia goes
Then, then (methinks) how sweetly flows
That liquefaction of her clothes.
Next, when I cast mine eyes and see
That brave vibration each way free;
O how that glittering taketh me!

poems.author: Edmund Waller
poems.title: On a Girdle
poems.text:
A narrow compass! and yet there
Dwelt all that's good, and all that's fair:
Give me but what this ribband bound,
Take all the rest the Sun goes round.

poems.author: Robert Herrick
poems.title: To Anthea, Who May Command Him Any Thing
poems.text:
Thou art my life, my love, my heart,
The very eyes of me,
And hast command of every part,
To live and die for thee.
poems.sourceHeading: TO ANTHEA WHO MAY COMMAND HIM ANY THING.

poems.author: Richard Lovelace
poems.title: To Althea, from Prison
poems.text:
When Love with unconfinéd wings
Hovers within my gates,
And my divine Althea brings
To whisper at the grates;
When I lie tangled in her hair
And fetter'd to her eye,
The birds that wanton in the air
Know no such liberty.

poems.author: John Gay
poems.title: Black-Eyed Susan
poems.text:
"O Susan, Susan, lovely dear,
My vows shall ever true remain
Let me kiss off that falling tear;
We only part to meet again.
Change as ye list, ye winds; my heart shall be
The faithful compass that still points to thee.

poems.author: Henry Carey
poems.title: Sally in Our Alley
poems.text:
Of all the girls that are so smart
There's none like pretty Sally;
She is the darling of my heart,
And she lives in our alley.
There is no lady in the land
Is half so sweet as Sally;
She is the darling of my heart,
And she lives in our alley.

poems.author: Samuel Rogers
poems.title: The Sleeping Beauty
poems.text:
Sleep on, and dream of Heaven awhile—
Tho' shut so close thy laughing eyes,
Thy rosy lips still wear a smile
And move, and breathe delicious sighs!

poems.author: Robert Burns
poems.title: Mary Morison
poems.text:
O Mary, at thy window be,
It is the wish'd, the trysted hour!
Those smiles and glances let me see
That make the miser's treasure poor:
How blythely wad I bide the stoure,
A weary slave frae sun to sun,
Could I the rich reward secure,
The lovely Mary Morison.

poems.author: Robert Burns
poems.title: Bonnie Lesley
poems.text:
To see her is to love her,
And love but her for ever;
For nature made her what she is,
And ne'er made sic anither!

poems.author: Robert Burns
poems.title: A Red, Red Rose
poems.text:
O my Luve's like a red, red rose
That's newly sprung in June:
O my Luve's like the melodie
That's sweetly play'd in tune.
As fair art thou, my bonnie lass,
So deep in luve am I:
And I will luve thee still, my dear,
Till a' the seas gang dry:

poems.author: Robert Burns
poems.title: Jean
poems.text:
I see her in the dewy flowers,
I see her sweet and fair:
I hear her in the tunefu' birds,
I hear her charm the air:
There's not a bonnie flower that springs,
By fountain, shaw, or green;
There's not a bonnie bird that sings
But minds me o' my Jean.

poems.author: Robert Burns
poems.title: John Anderson, My Jo
poems.text:
John Anderson my jo, John,
We clamb the hill thegither,
And mony a canty day, John,
We've had wi' ane anither:
Now we maun totter down, John,
But hand in hand we'll go,
And sleep thegither at the foot,
John Anderson my jo.

poems.author: William Cowper
poems.title: To Mary Unwin
poems.text:
Mary! I want a lyre with other strings,
Such aid from heaven as some have feign'd they drew,
An eloquence scarce given to mortals, new
And undebased by praise of meaner things,
That ere through age or woe I shed my wings
I may record thy worth with honour due,
In verse as musical as thou art true
And that immortalizes whom it sings:—

poems.author: William Cowper
poems.title: To Mary
poems.text:
Thy silver locks, once auburn bright
Are still more lovely in my sight
Than golden beams of orient light,
My Mary!

poems.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
poems.title: Love
poems.text:
All thoughts, all passions, all delights,
Whatever stirs this mortal frame,
All are but ministers of Love,
And feed his sacred flame.

poems.author: Lord Byron
poems.title: All for Love
poems.text:
O Fame!—if I e'er took delight in thy praises,
'Twas less for the sake of thy high-sounding phrases,
Than to see the bright eyes of the dear one discover
She thought that I was not unworthy to love her.
There chiefly I sought thee, there only I found thee;
Her glance was the best of the rays that surround thee;
When it sparkled o'er aught that was bright in my story,
I knew it was love, and I felt it was glory.

poems.author: Lord Byron
poems.title: There Be None of Beauty’s Daughters
poems.text:
There be none of Beauty's daughters
With a magic like Thee;
And like music on the waters
Is thy sweet voice to me:
When, as if its sound were causing
The charméd ocean's pausing,
The waves lie still and gleaming,
And the lull'd winds seem dreaming

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: Lines to an Indian Air
poems.text:
I arise from dreams of Thee
In the first sweet sleep of night,
When the winds are breathing low
And the stars are shining bright:
I arise from dreams of thee,
And a spirit in my feet
Hath led me—who knows how?
To thy chamber-window, Sweet!

poems.author: William Wordsworth
poems.title: She Was a Phantom of Delight

poems.author: Hartley Coleridge
poems.title: She Is Not Fair to Outward View
poems.text:
She is not fair to outward view
As many maidens be;
Her loveliness I never knew
Until she smiled on me.
O then I saw her eye was bright,
A well of love, a spring of light.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: I Fear Thy Kisses, Gentle Maiden

poems.author: Thomas Campbell
poems.title: Freedom and Love
poems.text:
How delicious is the winning
Of a kiss at love's beginning,
When two mutual hearts are sighing
For the knot there's no untying!

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: Love’s Philosophy
poems.text:
The fountains mingle with the river
And the rivers with the ocean,
The winds of heaven mix for ever
With a sweet emotion;
Nothing in the world is single,
All things by a law divine
In one another's being mingle—
Why not I with thine?

poems.author: Thomas Moore
poems.title: Echoes
poems.text:
Yet Love hath echoes truer far
And far more sweet
Than e'er, beneath the moonlight's star,
Of horn or lute or soft guitar
The songs repeat.

poems.author: Walter Scott
poems.title: A Serenade
poems.text:
The village maid steals through the shade
Her shepherd's suit to hear;
To Beauty shy, by lattice high,
Sings high-born Cavalier.
The star of Love, all stars above,
Now reigns o'er earth and sky,
And high and low the influence know—
But where is County Guy?

poems.author: John Keats
poems.title: Bright Star
poems.text:
No—yet still steadfast, still unchangeable,
Pillow'd upon my fair Love's ripening breast
To feel for ever its soft fall and swell,
Awake for ever in a sweet unrest;
Still, still to hear her tender-taken breath,
And so live ever,—or else swoon to death.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: One Word Is Too Often Profaned
poems.text:
I can give not what men call love;
But wilt thou accept not
The worship the heart lifts above
And the Heavens reject not:
The desire of the moth for the star,
Of the night for the morrow,
The devotion to something afar
From the sphere of our sorrow?

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: To a Lady, with a Guitar
poems.sourceHeading: TO A LADY, WITH A GUITAR.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: The Invitation
poems.text:
Best and Brightest, come away,
Fairer far than this fair day,
Which, like thee, to those in sorrow
Comes to bid a sweet good-morrow
To the rough year just awake
In its cradle on the brake.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: The Recollection
poems.text:
And still I felt the centre of
The magic circle there
Was one fair Form that fill'd with love
The lifeless atmosphere.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: Hymn to the Spirit of Nature
poems.text:
Life of Life! Thy lips enkindle
With their love the breath between them;
And thy smiles before they dwindle
Make the cold air fire; then screen them
In those locks, where whoso gazes
Faints, entangled in their mazes.
poems.sourceHeading: HYMN TO THE SPIRIT OF NATURE.

poems.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
poems.title: Music, When Soft Voices Die
poems.text:
Music, when soft voices die,
Vibrates in the memory—
Odours, when sweet violets sicken,
Live within the sense they quicken.
Rose leaves, when the rose is dead,
Are heap'd for the beloved's bed;
And so thy thoughts, when Thou art gone,
Love itself shall slumber on.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese I
poems.text:
And a voice said in mastery, while I strove,—
“Guess now who holds thee!”—“Death,” I said, But, there,
The silver answer rang, “Not Death, but Love.”

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese II
poems.text:
Men could not part us with their worldly jars,
Nor the seas change us, nor the tempests bend;
Our hands would touch for all the mountain-bars:
And, heaven being rolled between us at the end,
We should but vow the faster for the stars.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese VI
poems.text:
Thy touch upon the palm.  The widest land
Doom takes to part us, leaves thy heart in mine
With pulses that beat double.  What I do
And what I dream include thee, as the wine
Must taste of its own grapes.  And when I sue
God for myself, He hears that name of thine,
And sees within my eyes the tears of two.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese VII
poems.text:
The names of country, heaven, are changed away
For where thou art or shalt be, there or here;
And this . . . this lute and song . . . loved yesterday,
(The singing angels know) are only dear
Because thy name moves right in what they say.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese VIII
poems.text:
What can I give thee back, O liberal
And princely giver, who hast brought the gold
And purple of thine heart, unstained, untold,
And laid them on the outside of the wall
For such as I to take or leave withal,
In unexpected largesse? am I cold,

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese X
poems.text:
Yet, love, mere love, is beautiful indeed
And worthy of acceptation.  Fire is bright,
Let temple burn, or flax; an equal light
Leaps in the flame from cedar-plank or weed:

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XII
poems.text:
And love called love.  And thus, I cannot speak
Of love even, as a good thing of my own:
Thy soul hath snatched up mine all faint and weak,
And placed it by thee on a golden throne,—
And that I love (O soul, we must be meek!)
Is by thee only, whom I love alone.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XIII
poems.text:
And wilt thou have me fashion into speech
The love I bear thee, finding words enough,
And hold the torch out, while the winds are rough,
Between our faces, to cast light on each?—

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XIV
poems.text:
But love me for love’s sake, that evermore
Thou may’st love on, through love’s eternity.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XVI
poems.text:
And as a vanquished soldier yields his sword
To one who lifts him from the bloody earth,
Even so, Belovëd, I at last record,
Here ends my strife.  If thou invite me forth,
I rise above abasement at the word.
Make thy love larger to enlarge my worth!

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XVII
poems.text:
How, Dearest, wilt thou have me for most use?
A hope, to sing by gladly? or a fine
Sad memory, with thy songs to interfuse?
A shade, in which to sing—of palm or pine?
A grave, on which to rest from singing?  Choose.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XVIII
poems.text:
I never gave a lock of hair away
To a man, Dearest, except this to thee,
Which now upon my fingers thoughtfully
I ring out to the full brown length and say
“Take it.”  My day of youth went yesterday;

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XIX
poems.text:
The soul’s Rialto hath its merchandize;
I barter curl for curl upon that mart,
And from my poet’s forehead to my heart
Receive this lock which outweighs argosies,—

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XLII
poems.text:
I seek no copy now of life’s first half:
Leave here the pages with long musing curled,
And write me new my future’s epigraph,
New angel mine, unhoped for in the world!

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXI
poems.text:
Say over again, and yet once over again,
That thou dost love me.  Though the word repeated
Should seem a “cuckoo-song,” as thou dost treat it,
Remember, never to the hill or plain,
Valley and wood, without her cuckoo-strain
Comes the fresh Spring in all her green completed.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXIX
poems.text:
Nothing repels thee, . . . Dearest, teach me so
To pour out gratitude, as thou dost, good!

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese IV
poems.text:
And dost thou lift this house’s latch too poor
For hand of thine? and canst thou think and bear
To let thy music drop here unaware
In folds of golden fulness at my door?

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXV
poems.text:
My heavy heart.  Then thou didst bid me bring
And let it drop adown thy calmly great
Deep being!  Fast it sinketh, as a thing
Which its own nature does precipitate,
While thine doth close above it, mediating
Betwixt the stars and the unaccomplished fate.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXVI
poems.text:
Belovëd, what they seemed.  Their shining fronts,
Their songs, their splendours, (better, yet the same,
As river-water hallowed into fonts)
Met in thee, and from out thee overcame
My soul with satisfaction of all wants:
Because God’s gifts put man’s best dreams to shame.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXVII
poems.text:
My own Belovëd, who hast lifted me
From this drear flat of earth where I was thrown,
And, in betwixt the languid ringlets, blown
A life-breath, till the forehead hopefully
Shines out again, as all the angels see,
Before thy saving kiss!  My own, my own,
Who camest to me when the world was gone,
And I who looked for only God, found thee!

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXVIII
poems.text:
Said, Dear I love thee; and I sank and quailed
As if God’s future thundered on my past.
This said, I am thine—and so its ink has paled
With lying at my heart that beat too fast.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXIX
poems.text:
Because, in this deep joy to see and hear thee
And breathe within thy shadow a new air,
I do not think of thee—I am too near thee.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXI
poems.text:
Thou dove-like help! and when my fears would rise,
With thy broad heart serenely interpose:
Brood down with thy divine sufficiencies
These thoughts which tremble when bereft of those,
Like callow birds left desert to the skies.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXIII
poems.text:
Yes, call me by that name,—and I, in truth,
With the same heart, will answer and not wait.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXV
poems.text:
Yet love me—wilt thou?  Open thy heart wide,
And fold within, the wet wings of thy dove.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXVI
poems.text:
When we met first and loved, I did not build
Upon the event with marble.  Could it mean
To last, a love set pendulous between
Sorrow and sorrow?  Nay, I rather thrilled,

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XXXVIII
poems.text:
The third upon my lips was folded down
In perfect, purple state; since when, indeed,
I have been proud and said, “My love, my own.”

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XLI
poems.text:
Instruct me how to thank thee!  Oh, to shoot
My soul’s full meaning into future years,
That they should lend it utterance, and salute
Love that endures, from life that disappears!

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XLIII
poems.text:
How do I love thee?  Let me count the ways.
I love thee to the depth and breadth and height
My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight
For the ends of Being and ideal Grace.
I love thee to the level of everyday’s
Most quiet need, by sun and candlelight.

poems.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
poems.title: Sonnets from the Portuguese XLIV
poems.text:
Here’s ivy!—take them, as I used to do
Thy flowers, and keep them where they shall not pine.
Instruct thine eyes to keep their colours true,
And tell thy soul, their roots are left in mine.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 17
poems.text:
If I could write the beauty of your eyes,
And in fresh numbers number all your graces,
The age to come would say ‘This poet lies;
Such heavenly touches ne’er touch’d earthly faces.’

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 21
poems.text:
O! let me, true in love, but truly write,
And then believe me, my love is as fair
As any mother’s child, though not so bright
As those gold candles fix’d in heaven’s air:

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 24
poems.text:
Mine eye hath play’d the painter and hath stell’d,
Thy beauty’s form in table of my heart;
My body is the frame wherein ’tis held,
And perspective it is best painter’s art.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 27
poems.text:
Save that my soul’s imaginary sight
Presents thy shadow to my sightless view,
Which, like a jewel hung in ghastly night,
Makes black night beauteous, and her old face new.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 43
poems.text:
All days are nights to see till I see thee,
And nights bright days when dreams do show thee me.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 47

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 52
poems.text:
Blessed are you whose worthiness gives scope,
Being had, to triumph; being lacked, to hope.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 53
poems.text:
Speak of the spring, and foison of the year,
The one doth shadow of your beauty show,
The other as your bounty doth appear;
And you in every blessed shape we know.
In all external grace you have some part,
But you like none, none you, for constant heart.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 54
poems.text:
O! how much more doth beauty beauteous seem
By that sweet ornament which truth doth give.
The rose looks fair, but fairer we it deem
For that sweet odour, which doth in it live.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 56
poems.text:
Sweet love, renew thy force; be it not said
Thy edge should blunter be than appetite,
Which but to-day by feeding is allay’d,
To-morrow sharpened in his former might:

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 75
poems.text:
So are you to my thoughts as food to life,
Or as sweet-season’d showers are to the ground;
And for the peace of you I hold such strife
As ’twixt a miser and his wealth is found.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 91
poems.text:
Thy love is better than high birth to me,
Richer than wealth, prouder than garments’ costs,
Of more delight than hawks and horses be;
And having thee, of all men’s pride I boast:

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 98
poems.text:
Nor did I wonder at the lily’s white,
Nor praise the deep vermilion in the rose;
They were but sweet, but figures of delight,
Drawn after you, you pattern of all those.
Yet seem’d it winter still, and you away,
As with your shadow I with these did play.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 99
poems.text:
The forward violet thus did I chide:
Sweet thief, whence didst thou steal thy sweet that smells,
If not from my love’s breath? The purple pride
Which on thy soft cheek for complexion dwells
In my love’s veins thou hast too grossly dy’d.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 105
poems.text:
Kind is my love to-day, to-morrow kind,
Still constant in a wondrous excellence;
Therefore my verse to constancy confin’d,
One thing expressing, leaves out difference.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 115
poems.text:
Those lines that I before have writ do lie,
Even those that said I could not love you dearer:
Yet then my judgement knew no reason why
My most full flame should afterwards burn clearer.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 128
poems.text:
Since saucy jacks so happy are in this,
Give them thy fingers, me thy lips to kiss.

poems.author: William Shakespeare
poems.title: Sonnet 132
poems.text:
And truly not the morning sun of heaven
Better becomes the grey cheeks of the east,
Nor that full star that ushers in the even,
Doth half that glory to the sober west,
As those two mourning eyes become thy face:
